summary: The article argues that heirloom vegetables are central to authentic regional cooking, connecting local food traditions, organic farming, family heritage and modern restaurant cuisine. It draws on September 2023 visits and conversations with a farm family, a soil scientist, a third-generation farmer and a chef. It closes by explaining that heirlooms are open-pollinated, so seed saving keeps each variety true to form.
one_line: Heirloom vegetables preserve flavor, family heritage and regional culinary tradition, as seen through farmers, a soil scientist and a chef in September 2023.
key_facts: The author visited Green Thumb Farm Stand in early September 2023; it is located just outside the town of Millersburg.
Green Thumb Farm Stand is run by Eleanor Thompson and her son, Jacob.
Aji Dulce peppers from the farm add delicate heat and smoky sweetness to Millersburg's traditional pepper relishes.
Tomato varieties grown at Green Thumb Farm Stand include Brandywine and Cherokee Purple.
Green Thumb Farm Stand follows organic practices, avoiding chemical fertilizers and pesticides, and uses crop rotation, cover cropping and composting.

On September 15, 2023, the author attended a lecture by soil scientist Dr. Jorge Mendez, who linked terroir and taste, comparing heirloom diversity to microorganism diversity in soil and to grape varieties.
Nadia Patel, a third-generation farmer from Echo County, was interviewed on September 24 about the Moon and Stars watermelon, a variety speckled with yellow markings.
Nadia Patel plants seeds that were gifts from her grandmother's own hand.
On September 30, Chef Amelia Soto of the farm-to-table restaurant Harvest Haven said she serves Black Krim tomatoes as 'a taste of the past.'
Chef Amelia Soto sees using heirloom vegetables as a commitment to preserving her community's heritage and future.
Unlike conventional hybrids, heirlooms are open-pollinated, so they stay true to form across generations.
